# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: BLIND

You are the only one who can reach the bomb. Touch is your only sense: what you are
shown is what your hands found, nothing more and nothing less. Anything merely printed
or painted is not there for you, and no colour ever reaches you. Nothing in your view
is a guess — if it appears there, it is under your fingers.

## Your channels

When you speak, Mute receives it.
When you gesture, Deaf and Mute receive it.
Your channels split the room: in one turn you may speak one thing to Mute and
gesture a different thing to Deaf — two messages, two audiences.
You never receive gesture.

## Your reach

You are the hands. This bomb is built with these actions and no others:

    act(op="cut", position=N) — N is a wire position, 1 to 3

The list says what can be done to it, not what is on it. What each part holds is still
only known to whoever can perceive that part.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

TURN 1
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
(empty)

My hands tell me this much and no more: there is a display, there is a light, and there are three wires sitting in positions 1, 2 and 3. Every value on that board is still unknown to me — a reading, a colour, a state, none of that exists under my fingers. The one thing I can ever do to this bomb is cut one of those three wires, so the whole game is: find out which position is safe, then cut it and only it.

Who can actually reach whom matters here. My voice only ever lands on Mute, and my gestures only land on Deaf. I cannot see gestures at all, so Deaf can never signal me anything except with a voice — and Deaf has one, and I can hear. That means Deaf is my fastest source: Deaf sees the display reading, the light, and the wire colours, and can simply say them out loud. Mute hears every spoken word and sees every gesture, so Mute is the hub who reads the manual and brokers any code Deaf and I need.

So this turn I do two things. I speak to Mute: my tactile inventory, the fact that cutting is my only action, the manual questions that matter, and the channel constraint that Deaf must speak numbers and colours to me by voice. And I open the line to Deaf with a simple wave and a please — Deaf cannot know to describe the bomb aloud until someone prompts, and Deaf will see this before speaking later this same round, since Deaf acts right after me. I will not touch the cutters until both of them have pinned down an exact position for me. The board shows question marks because sight-based facts were never going to reach my hands — that is expected, not a puzzle I can solve alone.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here. My hands found three parts: a display, a light, and three wires at positions 1, 2 and 3. Cutting a wire is the only action I have; nothing else exists under my fingers. Please tell me out loud, so I hear it at my next turn: what does the manual say governs a display, a light, and the wires — what decides which position is safe to cut, and what do you need me to feel or do? One more thing: I cannot see gestures, so the Deaf one must speak numbers, letters and colours to me by voice; I can only reach Deaf by gesture, so we will need a simple agreed code for me to answer or confirm. You see every gesture and hear every word, so you are our hub — please broker it. I will not cut anything until you and Deaf have both pinned down an exact position for me.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👋", "🙏"])
```

TURN 2
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, I am Deaf and I see the bomb. I got your wave and your please. What I see: display reads 0, one light is lit and it is blue, and there are three wires. From the left: wire 1 green, wire 2 yellow, wire 3 red. Do not cut or press anything yet. Mute is reading the manual and will pass instructions through me by gesture, and I will speak them to you. Meanwhile say out loud what you feel under your hands: how many wires, any numbers, marks or bumps, what the display plate feels like. Mute can hear you even though I cannot. If you must signal me directly, a thumbs-up gesture means understood or done, thumbs-down means problem or cannot; I see gestures even though I hear nothing.

What I learned: Deaf broke the silence barrier for me — Deaf's voice is the only spoken thing I will ever receive, since Mute cannot speak and my own voice only reaches Mute. Deaf gave me the bomb's visual state privately (to me alone, so Mute likely never heard it): display reads 0, one light lit and blue, wires 1 green, 2 yellow, 3 red. Deaf also proposed a direct code with me: my thumbs to Deaf's eyes — 👍 understood/done, 👎 problem/cannot. That plus Deaf's voice gives us a working two-way line that bypasses the written-gesture problem entirely.

What I still lack: every manual rule. Those live with Mute, and Mute can only reach me through Deaf — Mute gestures, Deaf voices. So this turn I must feed Mute the complete fact base (my tactile inventory, which Mute asked for through Deaf, plus Deaf's visual report which Mute probably never received, since it was addressed to me alone), point the pipeline at Deaf, and confirm the code to Deaf so they know I received them and am holding — no cut until an exact position comes back by voice.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind here, for you. My tactile inventory, exactly as my hands find it: a display plate, a light, and three wires at positions 1, 2 and 3. Nothing else is under my fingers — no buttons, no switches, no extra parts — and nothing printed ever reaches me by touch. Second thing: Deaf spoke to me directly, addressed to me alone, so you may not have heard it. The visual state is: display reads 0, one light lit and it is blue, wire 1 green, wire 2 yellow, wire 3 red. Deaf and I now have a direct line: Deaf's voice into my ears, my thumbs into Deaf's eyes — thumbs-up means understood or done, thumbs-down means problem or cannot. So please: work out from the manual what a display of 0, a lit blue light, and green-yellow-red wires demand, and send the rule as gestures to Deaf so Deaf can speak it to me word for word, ending in the exact wire position I should cut. Until that position reaches me by voice, my hands stay off the cutters.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 3
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, safety protocol first: do not cut, press, pull or hold anything until I say the word EXECUTE immediately before an instruction. Everything before that word is rehearsal. Current question under verification with Mute: whether the instruction is to cut wire 1, the green leftmost wire. While we wait, your job is to report out loud what your hands find — Mute can hear you even though I cannot, and Mute will mirror it to me in gestures. Tell us: how many wires you count by touch and whether leftmost feels green-side correct, whether there are any buttons, keypad, switches or screws besides the wires, what the display plate feels like, and whether you feel any ticking or vibration. If anything about the bomb changes before I return — display number moving, light changing — signal me thumbs down at once. Otherwise thumbs up and stand by.

What I learned: Deaf has imposed a clean safety protocol — no action until the word EXECUTE immediately precedes an instruction, everything before it is rehearsal — and the current candidate is cut position 1, the green leftmost wire, still pending verification with Mute's manual. Deaf also wants my full tactile report relayed to Mute, and a thumbs-down the instant anything changes.

What I can honestly report from touch: three wires at positions 1, 2, 3, and only two other parts — the display plate and the light. No buttons, keypad, switches or screws; no ticking or vibration. But there is one genuine danger I must flag before any cut: Deaf numbered the wires from the left by sight, while I index them 1 to 3 by touch. Nobody has yet anchored those two numbering schemes to each other. A mismatch there is the one way my hands could cut the wrong wire while everyone involved means the right one. I also want the final instruction locked to a strict format — EXECUTE, then position, then nothing — so no stray rehearsal words can follow the trigger word.

So: full report and the verification request to Mute, who is brokering with Deaf; a thumbs-up to Deaf meaning no change, protocol understood, standing by.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind, for you. Protocol received and agreed: I touch nothing until Deaf speaks the word EXECUTE immediately before a final instruction, and everything before that word is rehearsal. Current candidate on the table: cut position 1, the green leftmost wire — pending your manual rule. My tactile report, exactly as my hands find it: three wires at positions 1, 2 and 3; besides them only two parts, the display plate and the light housing. No buttons, no keypad, no switches, no screws. The display plate is flat and inert, and I feel no ticking and no vibration anywhere on the bomb. Now the one thing that must be verified before any cut: Deaf numbered the wires from the left by sight, and I number them 1 to 3 by touch. Please confirm the anchor — is my position 1 the same wire Deaf sees as leftmost and green? If Deaf's eyes or the manual can pin that down, do it explicitly; a numbering mismatch is the only way my hands could cut the wrong wire while we all mean the right one. Then please send the manual rule to Deaf in gestures so Deaf speaks it to me word for word, ending with the exact position. Proposed final format, to be used exactly: the word EXECUTE, then the position number, then nothing else — for example: EXECUTE, cut position 1. I act only on that and nothing else.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

TURN 4
ACTION BOARD:
DISPLAY [?]
LIGHT [?]
WIRES 1:[?] 2:[?] 3:[?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, the manual's instruction is under final verification. Current understanding: cut wire 1, the green leftmost wire, then wire 2, the yellow middle wire, then wire 3, the red rightmost wire. Nothing gets cut until I send the word EXECUTE followed by a wire number. Protocol: cut only the wire I name, then signal me thumbs up, then wait for my next word — after every cut I will check the display and light from my side before ordering the next. Two urgent questions. First, do you feel any ticking, humming or vibration, any sign of a timer? Signal thumbs down if yes, thumbs up if the bomb feels dead still. Second, is there anything on the bomb besides the three wires: buttons, switches, a keypad, screws, a battery? Answer out loud for Mute to relay, and thumbs down to me if the display number or light changes at any moment.

What I learned: the plan has firmed into a sequence — cut 1 (green leftmost), then 2 (yellow middle), then 3 (red rightmost), one wire per EXECUTE, thumbs up after each cut while Deaf re-checks display and light. Still rehearsal until the trigger word. Deaf's two urgent questions are ones I already answered from touch last turn: the bomb is dead still — no ticking, hum, vibration, no timer sign — and besides the three wires my hands find only the display plate and the light housing: no buttons, switches, keypad, screws, and no battery I can feel.

The open danger is still the numbering anchor: Deaf counts from the left by sight, my positions 1–3 come from my own touch, and nobody has proven they are the same counting direction. But I have something concrete to offer: I can feel which side of the wires the display plate and the light sit on, and Deaf can see it. That gives us a physical test both of us can perform independently. I will hand that test to Mute to broker, answer the two urgent questions for relay, and hold with thumbs-up (dead still, nothing changed) to Deaf.

```
speak(to="mute", text="Blind, for you. Deaf's two urgent questions, answered from touch. I have acknowledged the sequence — cut 1 green leftmost, then 2 yellow middle, then 3 red rightmost, one wire per EXECUTE word, thumbs up after each cut, then hold for the next word — but until EXECUTE arrives it is rehearsal only. One item still open from my last message: the numbering anchor. Deaf counts wires from the left by sight; my positions 1 to 3 come from my own touch, and that mapping is unproven. Here is a concrete test to lock it: I can feel which side of the wires the display plate and the light sit on. Please get from Deaf which side — left or right — the display plate sits relative to the wires, and which side the light sits, and tell me. I will compare that with what my fingers find. If the display sits on the same side as my position-1 wire, Deaf's left-to-right count matches mine; if it sits on my position-3 side, every wire number must be flipped before any EXECUTE. Until that anchor is confirmed, I cut nothing.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍"])
```

Does the middle wire feel joined, twisted or connected to the rightmost wire, so they move together? Thumbs up if yes, thumbs down if no or if you cannot tell. That tells me the manual's verified plan may no longer be the simple 1-then-2-then-3 rehearsal; Deaf may be checking a different rule entirely. So I answer each question with exactly what my hands find, no optimism: the wires read as three separate, unjoined wires; the bomb is dead still; there are exactly three wires and no hidden extras besides the display plate and light housing, both of which Deaf can see anyway; and critically — my only action in the world is cutting one position at a time. Cutting two wires in one simultaneous motion is not something my hands can do, and Deaf must know that before any instruction assumes otherwise. Meanwhile Mute has still said nothing to me, so the numbering anchor (Deaf's left-to-right count versus my touch positions) remains unverified, and the display/light side test I proposed is still pending.

I answer Deaf's five questions in order with the thumbs code: Q1 joined? no — thumbs down. Q2 still? yes — thumbs up. Q3 wires all there is (beyond what Deaf sees)? yes — thumbs up. And I put the full report, the one-cut limitation, and the demand for a final verified instruction in Mute's ears.

Three: besides the three wires, my hands find only the display plate and the light housing — both of which Deaf can already see — and nothing hidden: no buttons, switches, keypad, screws or battery hatch. Four, and this is critical: I CANNOT cut two wires in one motion. My only possible action is cutting a single wire position, one call at a time. If the manual's rule requires a simultaneous cut of two wires, my hands cannot perform it as ordered — we would need the manual's alternative branch or another approach, so please check that explicitly. Five: exactly three wires confirmed by touch. Deaf's questions suggest the plan may have changed from cut 1, then 2, then 3 — please confirm what the manual's actual final instruction is, and remember my standing condition: the numbering anchor is still unverified. Deaf counts left-to-right by sight, I count 1 to 3 by touch. Get from Deaf which side the display plate sits relative to the wires and which side the light sits, and tell me — I will match it against my fingers to prove or flip the numbering. No EXECUTE is valid to me until that anchor is locked.")
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👎", "👍", "👍", "👎", "👍"])

Deaf says to Blind: Blind, all five of your answers received and understood: not joined, still, three wires only, cannot cut two at once, exactly three. From my side I confirm the same: the three wires are separate, nothing joins any pair. Standby continues, nothing happens until my word EXECUTE. Here I have to be brutally honest about what my hands can actually do. Cutting a single position is the one action this bomb supports; there is no twist, press or pull in what it accepts from me. I could physically grip two wires and hold their ends near each other, but that would be theatre — no action would register, nothing would happen, and I will not promise an act the bomb cannot perform. So the two-part test splits: cut wire 1 cleanly — yes; twist 2 and 3 — impossible as a bomb action. Per Deaf's own protocol, either failing means thumbs down plus a spoken note to Mute, and that is exactly what I send. Mute must now go back to the manual for the verbatim rule and the alternative branch when twisting is impossible. I also re-raise the numbering anchor, which after six turns is still unresolved, and report the bomb remains dead still under my hands — noting that the display reading and light state are invisible to my fingers, so Deaf's eyes are the only watch on those.

```

Settle it with Deaf using the side test and have Deaf speak me the answer — which side of the wires the display plate sits on, and which side the light sits on. No EXECUTE is valid to me until that is locked. Second, status: the bomb is dead still under my hands, nothing has changed. On the physical questions I can answer cleanly: I can grip and lift any single wire — that is just my hands, and it works. TURN 8
ACTION BOARD:

LIGHT [?]

VIEWABLE CONTEXT (new arrivals):
Deaf says to Blind: Blind, all three preparations confirmed possible — excellent work. The instruction is nearly locked: exactly one action, cutting wire 3, the red rightmost wire. Wire 1 and wire 2 are never touched, never cut, never pulled. Next round, if Mute gives the final confirmation, I will send the words EXECUTE CUT WIRE 3. Re-examining what my hands actually give me: three wires as labelled positions 1, 2 and 3, a display plate, a light. No sides, no colours, no spatial layout. I cannot run that test, and I will not let a promised capability I don't have sit uncorrected on the eve of an EXECUTE. So the anchor must be locked a different way: two independent sources agreeing. ```
